scenario: You're building a debris hut for a 40 F night with no sleeping bag. You are running low on daylight and can only do one part really well. Which layer matters most for preventing hypothermia?

options.text: A thick roof layer to block rain
Thick, dry debris packed under you - at least 6 inches after it is squashed flat
A leaf-stuffed door plug to block wind at the entrance
Extra leaves on the outside walls

explanation: You lie pressed against the cold ground all night, and that contact pulls heat out of you steadily - your clothing and any debris on top of you do little where your weight squashes them flat. A thick, dry bed under you is the first priority; make it deep enough that you cannot feel the ground once you lie on it. The roof, walls, and door plug all matter, and a full debris hut needs all of them (about 3 feet of debris overhead), but if time runs out, build the bed first. Lying on bare cold ground is a common way people get hypothermic even under a decent roof.

scenario: You need to choose a spot to build a shelter for a cold, rainy night in the woods. Rank these site checks from HIGHEST to LOWEST priority.

items.text: No dead trees or dead branches overhead within falling range
Not in a dry wash, ravine, or low spot that could flood
A natural windbreak on the upwind side (boulder, dense young trees)
Flat ground big enough to lie on
Water source within a short walk (but not right on the bank)

explanation: Falling dead wood and flash floods can kill you in your sleep with little or no warning, so those two checks always come first - and the NPS lists both as top campsite hazards. Wind is next because it strips body heat and can wreck a shelter, making hypothermia far more likely on a cold, wet night. Flat ground affects comfort and sleep, which matters but rarely kills. Water is important, but you can walk to it in the morning; about 200 feet away is ideal because it keeps you out of flood paths, damp air, and insect swarms.

scenario: You've built a quinzhee (hollowed snow mound) in a winter emergency and are settling in for the night with two other people. Snow is falling and you have a small backpacking stove. What is the most important thing to prevent overnight?

options.text: Frostbite from touching the snow walls
The vent and doorway getting sealed - especially if anyone lights the stove inside
Drips from the ceiling
Running out of snow to patch the walls

explanation: A snow shelter needs a constant supply of fresh air. Falling snow and frost can close the vent hole, and a fully blocked doorway traps stale, moist air. Burning fuel inside makes this deadly - a stove or candle produces carbon monoxide, which you cannot see or smell and which can kill sleeping people. Keep stoves outside, poke the vent open regularly with a stick or pole, and never fully seal the entrance. Wall contact can chill you but is not the main killer, and drips are a comfort problem you fix by smoothing the ceiling.

scenario: You have one 8x10 ft tarp, cord, and stakes. A strong, steady wind is driving rain across an open clearing from one direction, and only one small tree is nearby. Which pitch is the best choice?

options.text: A high, flat tarp roof tied at head height for maximum room
A plow point: one corner staked into the wind, the opposite corner raised on the tree, sides staked low
An open lean-to with the open side facing into the wind so smoke clears
Wrap the tarp around yourself and sit in the open

explanation: A plow point makes a low, pointed shape with its tip into the wind, so gusts and rain slide off it, and it needs only one anchor point. A high, flat tarp catches wind like a sail, flaps, and pools water. A lean-to with its open side into the wind funnels rain and wind straight in - the closed, sloped side must face the wind. Wrapping up in the open gives no protection from wind-driven rain and leaves you on the cold ground.

scenario: You are camping on frozen ground. You have an inflatable pad rated R 3 and a closed-cell foam pad rated R 2. Your sleeping bag is warm enough, but you were cold from below last night. What is the best move?

options.text: Use only the inflatable pad - the higher R-value one - and put the foam pad away
Stack both pads with no gap between them for about R 5 total
Put the foam pad on top of your sleeping bag instead of under you
Add another blanket on top of you; ground cold does not matter if the bag is warm

explanation: Pad R-values add together when stacked with no air gap, so R 3 plus R 2 gives roughly R 5 - much better for frozen ground. Many people put the foam on top because it warms up fast, and it also protects you if the air pad leaks. Insulation on top of you cannot fix cold from below: your bag is crushed flat under your body, so the pad does almost all the work against the ground. That is why a warm bag alone often leaves people cold on frozen ground.

scenario: Your hiking partner is shivering after a cold, wet afternoon. You have a mylar space blanket, a dry fleece jacket, and your pack. How do you use them best?

options.text: Wrap the space blanket directly on their wet clothes and have them lie on the ground
Get them sitting on the pack, swap wet layers for the dry fleece, then wrap the space blanket outside it with no gaps and their head covered
Save the space blanket for signaling and just keep walking to stay warm
Use the space blanket as a ground sheet and put the fleece over their legs

explanation: A space blanket blocks wind and wet and reflects some heat, but it is not insulation. It works best as an outer layer over dry clothing, sealed at the neck and wrapped with no gaps, with the person off the cold ground. In a 2016 test, wrapped torso models still cooled noticeably, just much less than uncovered ones - so add every bit of dry insulation you can. Lying on the ground undoes much of the benefit. Walking on while shivering and wet can worsen hypothermia; get help if they become confused or stop shivering while still cold.

scenario: Your car breaks down on a remote desert road at 11 a.m. It is 108 F. You have no cell signal, 2 gallons of water, a tarp, and the car. What should you do?

options.text: Walk to the last town you passed, 15 miles back, before it gets hotter
Sit inside the car with the windows rolled up to keep the sun off
Stay with the car, rig the tarp as shade on its shady side with an air gap, raise the hood, and rest until evening
Dig a deep trench right away to get out of the heat

explanation: Desert park rangers advise staying with a broken-down vehicle: it is shade, it holds your supplies, and it is far easier for searchers to spot than a person walking. A closed car in the sun gets dangerously hot within minutes. Hiking or digging in midday heat burns water and can cause heat stroke - do hard work only in the cooler morning, evening, or night. A tarp shade with an air gap and open sides lets air flow, and a raised hood signals that you need help.

scenario: It is a clear, calm, cold fall evening in hilly country. You are choosing where to build a shelter. Which spot is likely to be warmest overnight?

options.text: The flat meadow at the very bottom of the valley, next to the creek
The bare, exposed ridgetop above you
A small level bench partway up the slope, sheltered by trees, clear of dead limbs
A shallow hollow in the valley floor, out of sight of the trail

explanation: On clear, calm nights, cold, dense air drains downhill and pools in valley bottoms and hollows - the same process that makes valley fog form by dawn. Those low spots can be much colder and damper than ground a little higher. Ridgetops escape the cold pool but take the full force of the wind. A sheltered bench partway up the slope avoids both. The creekside meadow and the hollow also carry flood risk and extra condensation.

scenario: You are lost on a day hike, it is getting dark, and the temperature will drop near freezing. You have no shelter kit, but you have a phone with some battery, a warm hat, and a jacket. Put these actions in the best order.

items.text: Stop moving and call, text 911, or use satellite SOS if available
Get behind a windbreak that is clear of dead limbs and flood paths
Build a thick, dry bed of leaves or boughs to get off the ground
Put on all layers and pile more debris over yourself
At first light, move to an open spot and signal

explanation: Stopping first keeps you from getting more lost or hurt in the dark, and a call or satellite SOS while your battery lasts starts the search. Then get out of the wind using the first safe spot you find. The bed comes before piling debris on top because cold ground pulls heat out of you all night. Put on every layer and bury yourself in dry debris for insulation. At dawn, make yourself visible from the air and ground.

scenario: You are sleeping in a hammock under a tarp on a rainy 48 F night in wet woods. You are inside a good sleeping bag, but your back is freezing. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.text: The tarp is too high - lower it until it touches the hammock
Your body weight crushes the bag flat underneath you; add a pad inside the hammock or an underquilt below it
The hammock is hung too low; raise it 6 feet higher to get above the cold air
You need a thicker bag on top of you

explanation: In a hammock, the fabric and your weight squash the bag's insulation flat beneath you, and moving air under the hammock pulls heat away - so your back gets cold even when the top of you is warm. A sleeping pad inside the hammock or an underquilt hung under it fixes this. A tarp touching the hammock lets water wick through. Hanging higher increases fall risk and puts you in more wind. A thicker top layer does nothing for the compressed side under you.

start.scenario: It's 45 F with light rain. You have no shelter and no fire-starting gear. You have 90 minutes of daylight. What do you do first?

options.text: Start building a debris hut right away
Spend some time searching for natural shelter (cave, rock overhang)
Gather dry tinder and try to make a fire by friction

debris_hut.scenario: Good. You find enough dry leaves and branches, but the ground is soaked. Do you:

options.text: Build a thick bed of dry debris or boughs under you before finishing the roof
Lie on a thin layer of leaves and put all your effort into the roof

natural_search.scenario: After 15 minutes you find a shallow rock overhang. It is not deep enough to fully block the wind. Do you:

options.text: Use it as a windbreak, then pile a thick bed and debris around yourself
Keep searching for something better

fire_first.scenario: 45 minutes pass with no fire. You are wetter, tired, and daylight is almost gone. You have no shelter and no fire.
fire_first.explanation: In cold rain without reliable fire gear, shelter comes first. Hypothermia can set in well above freezing when you are wet. Friction fire in the rain is hard even for experts. Build shelter and a dry bed first; try fire only if time and dry material allow.

good_outcome.explanation: Correct. Cold, wet ground pulls heat out of you all night, so a thick, dry layer under you is essential - at least 6-8 inches after it compresses. Combined with a windbreak and debris over you, you make it to morning.

bad_outcome_cold.explanation: Even with a good roof, lying on a thin layer over wet ground drains your heat all night. Insulate from below first, then build up the roof and walls.

bad_outcome_dark.explanation: The overhang was good enough. Searching longer burns daylight and energy, and you end up in the dark with nothing. Take the first workable spot that is clear of dead limbs and flood paths, then improve it.

start.scenario: Three days into a widespread outage in mid-January. Nights drop to 18 F. You are in a 6-story apartment building with no power, heat, or water. You have 2 sleeping bags rated to 20 F, a propane camp stove with 1 canister, a hand-crank radio, and food for 5 days. Where do you shelter?

options.text: Stay in your 4th-floor apartment and work to hold in heat
Light the propane stove in the apartment for heat at night
Move into the building's stairwell - it's interior and protected

stay_4th_floor.scenario: Good. Neighboring units above, below, and beside you help buffer the cold. Which heat-saving step do you take first?

options.text: Try to keep the whole apartment warm by sealing every window
Move everyone and all bedding into the smallest room with few or no outside walls and close it off

seal_room.explanation: Sealing drafts helps, but trying to hold heat in the whole apartment spreads your body heat across too much space. Better: pick the smallest room, close it off, hang blankets over doors and windows, and sleep off the floor in your bags together. If it keeps getting colder, go to a warming center.

interior_room.explanation: Excellent. Concentrating people and body heat in one small, closed room is the most effective no-fuel strategy. Hang blankets over the door, sleep off the floor in your bags, wear hats and dry layers, and use the radio to find warming centers. Cook with the propane stove only outdoors, never inside.

stove_heat.explanation: Never use a camp stove, grill, generator, or gas oven to heat a home. CDC warns these produce carbon monoxide, an invisible, odorless gas that kills hundreds of Americans each year - often people asleep during outages. Use body heat, sleeping bags, and a small closed-off room instead, and go to a warming center if needed.

stairwell.explanation: Stairwells are poor places to sleep in the cold. Air moves up through them, pulling in cold air from below, and there is no small closed space to hold heat. They are also exit routes that must stay clear for fire safety. Stay in an enclosed unit with a closable door.
